articles.title: Find, skim, list, do, track

body.support:
Big jobs like getting your Ls feel hard. But they are just a list of small steps. Here’s how to do any of them.

1. **Find** the official website. For your Ls in Victoria, that’s **Transport Victoria**. Government sites end in **.gov.au**.
2. **Skim and scan.** Read the headings first. Find the parts for you, like “Who can apply” and “What to bring”. Skip the rest for now.
3. **List.** Write the steps in your own words, in order.
4. **Do.** One step at a time. Get your documents. Fill in the forms.
5. **Track.** Write down the date, any reference number, and the next step.
.
**Example: your Learner permit in Victoria**
- You must be at least **16**.
- You must pass the **learner permit test**.
- You need **proof of identity**, like a passport or birth certificate.
- There is a fee.
- If you’re under 21, you need **120 hours** of driving practice, with **20 at night**, before your P test.
.
Always check the official website. Rules and fees can change.
body.core:
Getting your Ls, a tax file number or your own bank account can feel like a mountain. But every piece of life admin is just a list of small steps, and the official website usually has the list. Here’s a method that works for any of them.

1. **Find** the official source. For a Victorian licence, that’s **Transport Victoria**. For tax, the **ATO**. Government sites end in **.gov.au**. Watch out for ads and copycat sites that charge you for free processes.
2. **Skim and scan.** Official pages are long, and most of it won’t apply to you. **Skim** the headings to see what’s there. **Scan** for the words that match your situation: your age, “first time”, “what to bring”, “fees”. Read those parts closely. Skip the rest for now.
3. **List.** **Paraphrase** the steps into your own words, as a numbered checklist, in the order you’ll do them.
4. **Do.** One step at a time: gather documents, book, fill in forms.
5. **Track.** Write down dates, **reference numbers** and the next step. It stops you losing your place, and it’s proof if something goes wrong.
.
**Example: your Learner permit in Victoria**
- You must be at least **16**.
- You need to pass the **learner permit knowledge test**.
- You need **proof of identity** documents, and there’s a fee.
- After that, learners under 21 need **120 hours** of supervised driving, including **20 at night**, before the probationary licence test.
.
Rules and fees change, so always check the official page before you start.
body.extend:
Adult life comes with a steady stream of admin: licences, tax, banking, Medicare, study, Centrelink. The process is different every time, but the method for tackling it isn’t.

1. **Find** the agency responsible and its official source. Licences in Victoria sit with **Transport Victoria**; tax with the **ATO**; Medicare and Centrelink with **Services Australia**. Check the domain (**.gov.au**) and be wary of ads and third-party sites that charge for free processes.
2. **Skim and scan for relevance.** Official guidance is written for everyone, so most of it won’t apply to you. **Skim** headings and summaries to map the page, then **scan** for the conditions that match your situation (age, first-time applicant, documents, fees). Read only those sections closely.
3. **List.** **Paraphrase** the relevant instructions into a short numbered sequence in your own words. If you can’t paraphrase a step, you don’t understand it yet: re-read it or ask.
4. **Do.** Complete one step at a time: gather documents, make bookings, complete forms accurately.
5. **Track.** Record dates, **reference numbers**, who you spoke to and what’s next. A simple log protects you if something is lost or disputed.
.
**Example: a Victorian Learner permit**
- Minimum age **16**; pass the **learner permit knowledge test**; provide **proof of identity**; pay a fee.
- Learners under 21 must then log **120 hours** of supervised driving, including **20 at night**, before the probationary licence test.
.
Eligibility rules and fees change, so the official page always overrides a summary, including this one.

caseStudies.title: No car, no driver? L2P

body.support:
In Victoria, learners under 21 need **120 hours** of driving practice before their P test.

But what if nobody in your family can drive with you? What if you don’t have a car?

The **TAC L2P** program helps. It is **free**. It gives learners a **volunteer mentor** and a **car** to practise in. The fuel is paid for.

It’s for learners aged **16 to 21** who don’t have a supervising driver or a car. Councils and community groups run it.

You can apply through your **myVicRoads** account.
body.core:
To get a P licence in Victoria, learners under 21 need to log **120 hours** of supervised driving. For many young people, that’s the hardest part. What if nobody in your family has a licence? What if you don’t have a car to practise in?

That’s why the **TAC L2P** learner driver mentor program exists. It’s **free**. It matches learners with a trained **volunteer mentor** and provides a **car** and fuel, so they can build up their hours.

L2P is for learners aged **16 to 21** (sometimes a little older) who don’t have a supervising driver or a car. The Transport Accident Commission (TAC) pays for it. Local councils and community groups run it.

You apply through your **myVicRoads** account. Many young people never find out it exists.
body.extend:
Victorian learners under 21 must log **120 hours** of supervised driving before they can take the probationary licence test. That rule assumes a learner has a licensed adult and a car. Many young people don’t.

The **TAC L2P** learner driver mentor program fills that gap. It’s **free**. It matches eligible learners with trained **volunteer mentors**, and provides a **car** and fuel, so they can build their hours safely.

L2P is aimed at learners aged **16 to 21** (in some cases older) who have no supervising driver or car. The Transport Accident Commission funds it, and local councils and community groups deliver it. Learners apply through their **myVicRoads** account.

It shows why skimming for eligibility matters. A learner who only read the main licence pages might never find out there’s a free program made for exactly their situation.

model.text:
**Job:** Open my first bank account.

**Official source:** the bank’s own website, not an ad.

**Skimmed for:** “under 18”, “what you need”, “fees”.

**My checklist**
1. Compare two youth accounts. Look for no monthly fees.
2. Check what ID I need. It’s my passport or birth certificate, plus my Medicare card.
3. Book a time at the branch, with a parent, because I’m under 18.
4. Open the account and set up the app.
5. Give my boss my BSB and account number.

**Tracking**
- 3 May: compared accounts. Picked one.
- 6 May: booked for 10 May.
- **Next:** find my passport.

teacher.overview: The boss course for Out & About. Students learn a five-step method for any piece of life admin (find the official source, skim and scan for relevance, list the steps in their own words, do them, track them), practise on a Victorian Learner permit example, and take a real process of their choosing as far as they can, keeping a tracker. The case study is the TAC L2P program, which provides free mentors and cars for learners without a supervising driver or vehicle.
prep: Check the official pages students are likely to use (Transport Victoria, ATO, Services Australia, banks) and that school filters allow them.
Send a note home: students may need ID documents or a parent for some steps. Nothing should be brought to school unless families agree.
Prepare 4–6 tricky problem cards for the Level Up (lost birth certificate, moved house, name doesn’t match ID, missed appointment).

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — The method
steps: **Hook (10 min):** list every piece of life admin students will face in the next three years.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Paraphrase and plan
steps: **Model (10 min):** paraphrase a dense paragraph into steps aloud.
**Say it in your own words (10 min).**

lessons.title: Lessons 3–4 — Sort it out
steps: **Do it (50 min):** skim, checklist, first steps; teacher conferences.
**Level Up (25 min):** tricky cases in groups.
**Check & reflect (25 min):** tracker review, quick check, reflection, sign-off.

teacher.answers:
**Sort:** who can apply — read; overseas licence — skip; proof of identity — read; heavy vehicles — skip; booking the test — read; motorcycle — skip.

**Annotation:** 1 summary (right page?); 2 eligibility (16+); 3 preparation (handbook, practice test); 4 documents (proof of identity); 5 cost and concessions; 6 next step (120 hours incl. 20 at night if under 21).

**Paraphrase (example):** 1 Make sure you’re 16 or older. 2 Read the Road to Solo Driving handbook and try the practice test. 3 Bring your original ID and the fee to your appointment. 4 Pass the knowledge test to get your permit.

**Case study:** some learners have no licensed adult or car; L2P is for 16–21-year-olds without a supervising driver or car and gives a free mentor, car and fuel; find it by skimming official licence pages for support or eligibility, or asking the council’s youth services.

realityCheck: **Students will be at very different starting points.** Some already have their Ls; some have no ID documents at all. Let them choose a process that’s real for them, and accept “as far as you can” honestly.
**ID documents are precious.** Don’t ask students to bring originals to school. Steps that need originals can happen at home or at the agency.
**Under-18s often need a parent or carer.** Plan for that: some steps become homework with a family member.
**Rules and fees change.** The course deliberately points to the official page; check the Learner permit details each year before teaching.
**Works in a real class:** yes, and it’s one of the most valued courses. Students often finish a real task (a TFN, a bank account) they’d been putting off.

levels.support: Aimed at about Year 5 reading: shorter article and case study, 6 key words, word bank, a simpler process option and step prompts.
levels.core: Aimed at about Year 7 reading: the standard version with skimming and scanning, paraphrasing, the info page, L2P and a tracked real process.
levels.extend: Aimed at about Year 9 reading: agency responsibility, paraphrasing dense official language, eligibility as a way to find support, and group problem-solving.
